title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6: fishermen analogy — elect makes apostles/faithful, not prior trade/poverty
pass_a_gloss: which will be clear from a not dissimilar example. If we say God chose fishermen as his Apostles, in this way of speaking "to choose" is the same as "to make an Apostle"; it does not, however, signify "to make fishermen," because by their own will they had already been made fishermen before they were elect Apostles. So when I say God chose the poor rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, "to choose" is the same as "to make believers and heirs of the kingdom," but it is not the same as "to make them poor"; because then they are supposed already poor when they are gifted with faith and adoption unto the heavenly kingdom.
pass_b_english: a near parallel shows why. If we say God chose fishermen as his Apostles, "choose" there means make them Apostles — not make them fishermen. They were already fishermen by their own trade before they were elect Apostles. So when I say God chose the poor who are rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, "choose" means make them believers and kingdom-heirs — not make them poor. Poverty is already assumed when faith and adoption to the heavenly kingdom are given.
source_text: quod exemplo non dissimili patebit. Si dicamus Deum elegisse piscatores Apostolos suos, in hac loquendi formula eligere est idem quod facere Apostolum; non autem significat facere piscatores, quia prius sua voluntate erant facti piscatores, quam electi Apostoli: Sic cum dico Deum elegisse pauperes divites in fide & heredes regni, eligere est idem quod facere fideles & regni heredes, sed non est idem quod facere pauperes; quia tum supponuntur pauperes cum donantur fide & adoptione ad regnum coeleste.
